#9773. Finite State Raises $27 Million to Help Device Makers Fight ‘Vulnpocalypse’ with AI-Powered Product

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

Columbus, Ohio, United States, November 10th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--Finite State, a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices.

Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure. The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure.

The new capital will expand Finite State’s already global operations, deepen its presence across key international markets, and accelerate development of the platform’s autonomous capabilities. These investments will enable more manufacturers around the world to uncover the gap between the software they plan to ship and what actually runs in the finished device, and to continuously identify and mitigate security risks across increasingly complex software supply chains.

The funding comes at a turning point for product security. In October, AI-powered research uncovered critical flaws in some of the world’s most widely used software, including a vulnerability in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the web, in a surge security leaders have dubbed the “Vulnpocalypse.” AI has shrunk the time it takes to find a flaw and turn it into an attack from weeks to days, and sometimes hours. Connected devices are especially exposed: a single flaw in a shared open-source component can sit inside millions of shipped products that are hard to inventory and slow to patch. For manufacturers, the urgent question is no longer whether a vulnerability exists. It is which of their products contain it.

In parallel, regulators worldwide now expect connected products to be secure by design, with security built in and demonstrated before a device ships rather than added after it reaches the market. The EU Cyber Resilience Act, FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, UNECE R155 and R156 for vehicles, and IEC 62443 for industrial systems all place the burden of proof on the manufacturer, and the cost of falling short includes blocked market access, recalls, and liability.

Meeting that standard is difficult because modern connected products are assembled, not written from scratch. A single device can contain open source libraries, third-party components, and legacy code from many suppliers, and what ships in the finished firmware often differs from what the source code and bill of materials describe. Manufacturers cannot secure what they cannot see.

“Every connected product—cars, infusion pumps, toys, OT, baby monitors, your home router—runs on third-party code and components, making inspection and security exceptionally challenging,” said Mike Venerable, Founding Partner, The O.H.I.O. Fund. “Governments worldwide are imposing new regulatory pressures on manufacturers, recognizing how quickly AI-enabled attackers can exploit vulnerabilities. Finite State is solving an incredibly difficult product and technology security challenge by deploying a platform that has earned the trust of investors and customers. We are delighted to support Finite State through this financing and believe the company will be an important solution for connected device security and supply chain risk mitigation.”“Moments like this separate the companies built for what’s coming from those still catching up,” said Brittany Blanco, Innovation Banking Director II, CIBC Innovation Banking. “We’re excited to back a team that saw this shift early and is ready to meet it on a global scale.”

Finite State customers span the world’s critical infrastructure and connected device ecosystem—from national power grids and a U.S. national security research laboratory to global automakers, life-saving medical devices, and the connected hardware running inside homes, hospitals, and factories worldwide. With the IoT security market projected to reach $80.3 billion by 2031,[1] Finite State’s growing international customer base reflects a challenge that increasingly transcends borders: manufacturers must understand exactly what software is inside their products, whether it can be exploited, and what they need to do about it.

Bruce Lin, Senior Manager, Software Department at JET OPTOELECTRONICS CO., LTD., a Tier 1 supplier of automotive electronics and smart cockpit solutions serving global automakers, said: "The depth of Finite State's binary and firmware analysis, the insight it yields into what's in a shipped device and not just the build manifest, the direct and transitive dependency visibility, and audit-ready compliance mapped to the regulations we actually face, are all invaluable."Finite State founder and CEO Matt Wyckhouse said: “The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it. Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers. This Series C round will enable our talented team to both drive the next generation of remarkable platform advances and expand our global reach to safeguard both our customers and theirs.”

Among its latest honors, Finite State was named to the 2026 Inc. 5000, an annual ranking of the fastest-growing private companies in America, and chosen as a finalist in SiliconANGLE’s prestigious 2026 TechForward Awards in the Security category.

Finite State empowers device OEMs to ship securely while enabling engineering teams to move at the speed of AI, immediately transforming product artifacts into audit-ready assurance through a single automated workflow. Leveraging deep binary analysis and AI-native execution, the platform unifies code, compiled components, and firmware in minutes—connecting security design with deployed software. By continuously generating SBOMs, VEX, and signed compliance packages, Finite State enables connected device companies across industries such as medical devices and automotive to meet evolving regulations, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), and deliver continuous compliance at speed.

#9772. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi/T)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​/T)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable (X) representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.10)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.10)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.10)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with (K) options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where ($p_{\max}$) is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.80:

C=3(0.99)−12=0.98 C=\frac{3(0.99)-1}{2}=0.98 C=23(0.99)−1​=0.98

Notice that the winning probability is 0.99, but the reported confidence is 0.98. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

#9770. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9768. OffSec Celebrates 20 Years of Practitioner-Built Training From the Creators of Kali Linux and OSCP

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

New York, USA, November 10th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--Kali Linux. OSCP. Try Harder. For 20 years, OffSec has set the standard for the tools security practitioners use, the skills they prove, and the mindset they bring to the work. This month OffSec is marking its 20th anniversary as a global leader in hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications for individuals and enterprise security teams.

"Our founders built an incredible brand and an incredible product,” said OffSec CEO Ning Wang. “Our mission has stayed the same. We develop critical thinkers, cyber warriors, and problem solvers who are ready to excel in their jobs under stress. Hands-on is the only way we believe you can effectively train someone.”

OffSec began in 2006 when cybercrime was becoming big business. OffSec grew out of the security community, founded by practitioners who believed the best way to teach cybersecurity was to share what they'd learned through hands-on experience. That origin story still shapes how OffSec develops cybersecurity practitioners and teams. Through hands-on training with real systems, learners build practical skills, strengthen their problem-solving abilities, and gain the confidence to tackle challenges when the obvious approach fails.

BackTrack Linux brought penetration testing tools together in one open-source platform. In 2013, OffSec rebuilt it as Kali Linux, a free environment for penetration testing, research, forensics, and reverse engineering. In 2023, Kali Purple extended it to defenders.

OSCP earned its reputation as the gold standard in penetration testing certifications because candidates must work through live systems, adapt their approach, and document what they accomplish. Employers trust it as evidence of real capability. For many practitioners, it is a career-defining milestone. OSCP+ added a renewable credential in 2024. Now, for a limited time, individual practitioners can save 20% off of Learn One annual subscription.

The Research and Practice They Learn From

In 2009, OffSec launched the Exploit Database, a non-profit, public-service archive of public exploits, proof-of-concept (PoC) code, shellcode, and security papers, which it still maintains as a free resource. It also acquired the open-source training project VulnHub, offers free labs in Proving Grounds Play, and recently added HackTrack. HackTrack offers live weekly training over a 10-week stretch. The first round of HackTrack focused on OSCP and was offered free to those with a Learn One or Course and Certification Bundle. A new HackTrack focused on OSAI is set to launch soon.

Along the way, Try Harder became the security community's shorthand for the persistence and dedication that a career in cybersecurity demands. In October 2026 at Singapore International Cyber Week, CEO Wang urged her Women in Cyber keynote audience to do hard things early that build confidence and resilience, noting, “If you don’t struggle through something, you will never become really great at it,” she said.

Attackers now use AI to discover and weaponize vulnerabilities at speeds unimaginable 20 years ago. The time between a vendor patch and a working exploit continues to shrink. Cybersecurity skills gaps remain a growing challenge. According to ISC2’s 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, 95% of organizations report at least one skills gap, with 59% describing those gaps as critical or significant, up from 44% in 2024. These findings reinforce the need to move beyond once-a-year training toward continuous, hands-on skill development, an approach rooted in OffSec’s philosophy since day one.

“Frontier AI models are evolving at unbelievable speed. If you don’t keep up, you won’t be able to do the job,” said CEO Wang. “Certification still assesses capability. But you need to constantly upskill your teams so they are ready to defend your organization. It is simply no longer a nice-to-do. It’s a must-do.”

OffSec has grown from a specialist offensive security provider into a full cybersecurity learning and workforce development portfolio. Every course teaches the why, the what, and the how so practitioners learn to think through problems they have never seen. Through Learn Enterprise, OffSec’s hands-on training platform for enterprise security teams, organizations bring that approach to every member of their security team. The platform includes:

In 2026, OffSec added Live Training, which brings its instructors on site to work with security teams in realistic scenarios. OffSec has provided this training to more than two dozen organizations and hundreds of learners.

CEO Wang calls AI-era learning OffSec’s top priority. “To fight AI you have to use AI,” said CEO Wang. “Your red team and your blue team both need to be AI literate. Next year, we will release new and updated courses that modernize our training for the AI age.”

Preview OffSec's Learn Enterprise platform, then request a personalized demo to explore how it can support your team’s training goals at: https://www.offsec.com/business/enterprise-solutions/.

#9767. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

#9765. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9764. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9761. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9760. The draw is 24% of the outcomes and 0.8% of the labels: auditing class collapse in a three-way model

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at soccerdreamai.com

A three-class classifier that reports one label per row is not a three-class classifier. It is a ranking function collapsed to a decision, and the collapse is where the information dies. On our platform, 11,177 of 46,189 settled predictions ended in a draw; the label draw was emitted 360 times.

Every number below comes from the live production table, queried today, not estimated.

The base table stores one row per model per match with the realised outcome attached. Two distributions matter: what happened, and what the model said would happen. If the second is a faithful compression of the first, they should be close.

The draw happens 24.20% of the time and is named as the sole answer 0.78% of the time — a 31× under-representation. 16,925 rows name it as one of two outcomes; 27,647 rows chose strictly between home and away and could not be correct if the match finished level.

That last set is the interesting one. Of those 27,647 binary picks, 6,269 (22.68%) finished level. The ceiling was set by the label vocabulary, not the analysis.

Reported accuracy by output arity on rows with a settled outcome:

58.52% on single-label rows looks like a margin over chance. But chance for a 44/31/24 class split under a majority-class strategy is 44.26% — and the "single" bucket is not homogeneous: 4,490 of those rows had a compound single label (home/draw, away/draw) and 27,647 were strictly two-class. Averaging them reports neither.

This is a binary classifier wearing a three-class schema: any binary classifier over football outcomes pays a fixed 22.68% tax on the subset it is applied to. A genuine three-class system moves that tax into calibrated probability on the draw.

Aggregate accuracy is what lets this bug live for 46,000 rows. Per-class precision and recall make it visible in one screen:

Result on the 45,860 rows with a non-null outcome:

Draw precision of 26.81% hides the shape of the failure: draw alone hit 78 of 360 (21.67%), while away/draw hit 5,920 of 10,997 (53.83%) and home/draw hit 3,272 of 5,928 (55.20%). The compound labels are not predicting a draw — they express uncertainty between two outcomes, and the draw is an escape hatch. Recall on the draw is 41.16%: 6,576 draws were named by no label at all.

The most damning row: 283 distinct models emitted draw at least once across 46,189 predictions, and the busiest did it 4 times. No model here has learned to identify draws. Some occasionally guess.

Accuracy cannot compare a one-hot label with a distribution. Log loss can. The emitted label is scored as a probability vector (1.0 on the named class, split evenly for compounds) against the market-implied probability from the quoted three-way price, normalised to sum to one. 45,110 of 46,189 rows survive the price sanity filter.

Log loss 0.9683 for the market-implied probabilities, 13.4625 for the emitted label — a factor of 13.9. That is what a zero looks like inside a logarithm: every row where the model picked a compound and the outcome was the excluded class contributes -log(0), clamped at 1e-12, or 27.6 nats.

This is not a claim that market probabilities are a good model. It is a claim about representation: a probability vector can be scored and improved; a one-hot label can only be counted, and counting rewards the majority class. The draw Brier of 0.1812 is what a real three-class output would have to beat.

If confidence carried draw-risk signal, high-confidence binary picks would convert to draws less often. They don't. Draw rate among single picks restricted to home or away (27,647 rows, 6,269 draws):

Flat, and mildly inverted at the top: a model that says 9 is no less likely to be level than one that says 4. That is the expected failure when confidence is attached to a binary comparison and the third class was pruned before scoring — the pruning discards the evidence.

The market-implied draw probability, on the same 45,110 rows, is calibrated in the ordinary sense:

Mean implied 0.2423 against an observed 24.20%. The information is already in a column we store, and it is thrown away at the label step.

Draw rates are not uniform across competitions. On 78,553 finished matches the overall draw rate is 24.69% (19,392 draws), and competition buckets with at least 500 settled rows span 15.49% to 30.42%:

A single global threshold for "is this a draw?" is therefore wrong by about 15 percentage points. A per-class correction must be conditioned on the competition, and that requires a calibrated probability rather than a relabelled decision — you cannot attach a competition prior to a one-hot output.

The 46,189 settled predictions cover 16,724 distinct matches, and only 3,736 (8.09%) join to matches on id; the rest carry a match_id from an older identifier space. Every per-competition number above was computed from matches directly — joining predictions to competitions would have dropped 92% of rows and produced a confident, wrong table.

Second: 329 settled rows have actual_result IS NULL and 121 have hit IS NULL while settled is true. They are excluded explicitly with FILTER.

A 24% versus 0.8% gap is not a dataset problem. Twenty-four percent is an ordinary share for the third class of a football outcome. The imbalance was manufactured by the output format: the model emitted a label, the vocabulary had three slots, and the scoring loop only rewarded the slot that appeared most. Fixing it needs no better model — three numbers instead of one string, and a refusal to ship a three-class system whose per-class recall is never measured for one of its classes.

The draw was never hard to predict. It was hard to record.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

#9756. Reddit Reviews Landed With 161 Comments and Zero Upvotes

Reddit's announcement post for Reddit Reviews is sitting at zero votes. The comment section under it has 161 replies.

That ratio is the review. Zero up, 161 down.

And it was written by the people who actually run the site's communities.

The feature is simple enough. Reddit used AI to pull product talk from across subreddits and pack it into about 10,000 product pages. Electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, apparel, US only.

You search a product, and you get a "what people are saying" block. Positive, mixed, negative split, plus topic filters.

And every summary links back to the original threads.

Fine idea on paper. Reddit has been the place people go to ask whether an air fryer is worth it for a decade. This just puts a label on it.

The top one, at 114 points, is from a user called judasblue. "Yeah, this definitely isn't going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site."

"Oh those advertising spam accounts are giving you consistent issues? What if instead of dealing with them we intentionally built them features to make THEIR jobs easier?"

That is the mood. Not curiosity. Not "cool, shopping."

Just a long tired sigh from people who spend their evenings deleting bots.

i went looking for the beta timeline first, because it explains a lot. Reddit tested this since February with a small group of US users in electronics, video games, and health and beauty.

And in September it added home and garden plus apparel. Now it is open to every US user.

There is also product info with images, prices, and where to buy links. Reddit says that data comes from brand and retailer catalogs. The early testing ran in places like r/espresso and r/skincareaddiction, where people already argue about grinders and moisturizer for free.

That last part is what nobody in the thread liked. Price and buy links turn a conversation into a store shelf.

brandy_mcstyle from Reddit's product marketing team answered concerns directly in the thread. The defense has two parts.

Reddit excludes comments from accounts labeled as apps. And it defines a "review conversation" as a comment that appears to describe personal experience with a product.

A user named DeltaJesus replied with the obvious thing.

"So exactly what these bots are already doing now?"

He is right. Astroturfing has never looked like a press release.

It looks like a person saying they owned the thing for six months and it changed their life. Filtering for personal experience filters for the exact shape of a paid comment.

Reddit's answer to fake reviews is a detector tuned to copy the fakes.

Four separate mods asked how to turn this off for their subreddits. Beeb294, Sillvaro, SecureThruObscure, and LindyNet all wanted an off switch. None of them got one.

judasblue asked the sharper version. If Reddit is not making money from this feature, why not let non commercial subs opt out? He called the absence of a switch "sus," which is about as polite as that thread gets.

CouncilOfStrongs, a mod of over ten years, put the trust problem in one line. "There has been zero noticeable reduction in spam volume in the over 10 years I have been a moderator on this platform."

And WalkingEars added the detail that stings. Subs without aggressive moderation are now full of "insipid LLM posts that read more like LinkedIn than Reddit."

Follow the money, or the missing money. Reddit's shares dropped 29% after investors got spooked about Google's AI Overviews eating referral traffic from search. The company is also moving toward a logged in experience, which keeps people on site instead of letting search engines index everything for free.

Reddit Reviews lands weeks later, right before holiday shopping. That timing is not subtle.

Reddit also says it earns no commission on those buy links. Maybe true today. A shopping surface with 130 million daily users and live price data does not usually stay commission free for long.

The line that stuck with me is buried in the announcement. Half of US shoppers say they come to Reddit to validate AI recommendations.

Read that twice. People ask a model for advice, then come to Reddit to check whether the model lied. Reddit's new feature hands them an AI summary of the human answers they came for.

The loop closes on itself. Ask a model, verify with a model that read people, then buy.

i do not think Reddit is evil for this. i think it is a company with a traffic problem building a shopping product, because shopping products make money.

But the packaging is what annoys me. This is not a community tool. It is a storefront wearing a community tool's jacket.

Somewhere in the middle of all this i remembered my own review habit. i read the two star reviews first, always. Not the one stars, those are people having a bad day with a delivery driver.

The two stars are where the real complaints live. The hinge that loosened after four months. The app that stopped syncing.

And i once spent forty minutes in a rice cooker thread because one commenter had measured the actual temperature variance across three units with a probe. No brand. No affiliate link.

Just a guy with a thermometer and a grudge.

That is the thing Reddit Reviews cannot summarize. The grudge. The guy who measured.

A summary keeps the verdict and throws away the obsession that made it worth reading.

If you already search Reddit by adding "reddit" to your Google query, this feature is not for you. You will find the thread anyway, and you will read the messy parts that a summary flattens.

If you are the kind of shopper who reads one product page and calls it research, this will feel like a shortcut. And it mostly is one, for better and worse.

The people who should actually care are the mods. They get the spam risk, the extra moderation load, and no switch to turn any of it off. The feature benefits the shopper who never opens Reddit and costs the volunteer who keeps it usable.

That trade is bad. Not complicated. Just bad.

The comment i keep coming back to is from TGotAReddit, replying to Reddit's claim that nobody pays for placement. "Well if you don't benefit and the advertisers don't benefit, who does this benefit? Because it's not gonna help mods or users."

i keep thinking about the zero votes. Reddit built a review machine for ten thousand products and its own users could not bring themselves to click the up arrow on the announcement.

Maybe that is the most honest review on the page.

#9752. Progressive Web Apps vs Native App: When a PWA Is Enough

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev

Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.

If you are weighing progressive web apps vs native app development, the short answer is this: a PWA is enough when your users mostly work in the foreground, on screens you control, and you need one codebase with fast updates. Go native (or React Native) when you depend on background work, deep hardware access, or iOS features that Safari still does not expose. Below is how to tell which side of that line your product sits on, based on current browser support data and on building an offline-first restaurant POS that runs in the browser.

A progressive web app is a website that can behave like an installed app. Technically it is still a web page running inside a browser engine, but it adds two things:

Once installed, a PWA gets its own icon and opens in its own window without the browser address bar. To the user it feels like an app. Under the hood, the browser is still doing the work, and that is the root of every limitation discussed below.

A native app, by contrast, is built for the operating system directly (Swift/Kotlin, or a cross-platform toolkit like React Native or Flutter that compiles to native components) and is distributed through the App Store or Google Play.

The rows that matter most are the bottom four. Everything above them is where PWAs usually win.

Most "PWA vs native" decisions are really "how much do we care about iPhone users?" decisions. Android with Chrome supports far more of the web platform than iOS does. I checked MDN's browser compatibility data in November 2026, and these are the gaps that most often push a project toward native:

Safari on iOS added the Push API in version 16.4, but MDN notes it only works for web apps saved to the Home Screen. A user who just visits your site in Safari cannot get push messages. That means your onboarding has to talk people through "Share, then Add to Home Screen" before notifications even become possible.

On Chrome and Edge, your app can listen for the beforeinstallprompt event and show its own "Install app" button at a sensible moment. Safari does not support that event, and MDN states plainly that this technique does not work on iOS. Installing is entirely manual for iPhone users. Since iOS 16.4, they can at least do it from the Share menu in Safari, Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Orion, not only Safari.

The Background Synchronization API lets a service worker retry a failed request once the connection returns, even after the user has closed the tab. Periodic Background Sync and Background Fetch go further. According to MDN's compatibility data, Safari supports none of these. On iOS, your app can only sync while it is open.

Web Bluetooth, WebUSB and Web Serial exist in Chromium browsers but not in Safari. If your product needs to talk to a card reader, label printer, scale or other peripheral from an iPhone or iPad, a PWA alone cannot do it.

Check the EU caveat: Historically every iOS browser had to use WebKit, so Chrome on iPhone had Safari's limits. MDN notes that since iOS 17.4 Apple allows other browser engines in the EU, so behaviour there can differ. Test on the devices and regions your customers actually use.

Offline-first apps live or die on local storage, so this deserves its own section. Small key-value data can go in localStorage, which is capped at about 5 MiB per origin. Anything serious (orders, products, customers) belongs in IndexedDB, usually through a library rather than the raw API.

MDN's storage guide gives the current quota rules:

The bigger risk is not quota, it is eviction. By default, browser data is "best-effort", meaning the browser may delete it under storage pressure. Safari goes further: with cross-site tracking prevention on, it removes script-created data for origins the user has not interacted with in the last seven days of browser use. When eviction happens, the whole origin's data goes at once.

And the rule that matters more than any API call: local data must never be the only copy of anything important. Sync it to a server as soon as a connection is available, and design the app so a wiped device can rebuild itself from the server.

I spent about two years as a senior frontend engineer on Oscar, a point of sale system for restaurants and retail in Pakistan. It is a React web app, not a store app, and it had to keep taking orders, printing receipts and sending tickets to the kitchen even with the internet down. A few things that experience taught me about when the web is enough:

The browser handled offline data well. Oscar keeps its data in a local WatermelonDB database on browser storage, so the POS works the same with or without a connection, and nobody has to install anything. Changes sync to a Django backend when the connection returns, and the server stays the source of truth for reporting. I wrote more about that architecture in Offline-First POS: Lessons From Building Oscar in React.

Real-time features need an offline plan of their own. Orders reached the kitchen display system over WebSockets. Every feature like that needs a decision, made at design time, about what happens when the socket drops.

Hardware was the hard part. Restaurants need receipt, kitchen and bar printers. Oscar connects to local printers through QZ Tray, a printer bridge, and I built the routing so each ticket lands on the right printer: receipts at the counter, tickets in the kitchen, drinks at the bar. That pattern (a web app plus a local helper for hardware) is a useful middle ground, but it is one more component to set up and support.

The broader lesson: Oscar ran on counters and devices the business controlled, in the foreground, all shift long. That is the ideal case for a web app. A consumer app that must wake up in the background on a stranger's iPhone is the opposite case.

Answer these honestly. If most of your answers land on the left, a PWA (or a plain responsive web app) is probably the right first build.

For most early-stage products, start on the web. A well-built responsive web app with a manifest and a service worker covers desktop, Android and most iPhone use, can be found on Google, and costs less to build and maintain than separate native apps. If you hit a real platform wall (background work, hardware, iOS push at scale), you can add a React Native app later and reuse your backend, API and much of your business logic.

The mistake to avoid is choosing a PWA and then discovering the iOS gaps after launch. Write down the device features your product depends on, check each one against current browser support, and prototype the riskiest one first.

If you are planning an offline-first app or a POS and want a second opinion on web vs native, take a look at my product development service or the React development service, or see how the Oscar POS case study handled it.

I'm Muhammad Moiz, a full-stack developer who builds web apps, SaaS and POS systems, and takes AI-built apps (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) to production. Get in touch.

#9749. Full App Backup for Game Receipts: Node.js Nightly Job, User Uploads, Object Storage

Short answer: treat a nightly game-app backup as one recoverable run containing the database dump, the original receipt files, and a manifest that names both; use private object storage, immutable run prefixes, and a restore drill before calling the job complete.

The important decision is access control versus delivery simplicity. Receipt images and purchase records are related evidence, not two independent exports. A public object URL may be easy for a client to consume, but it is a poor default for audit material. A private bucket with short-lived, server-issued access takes more application work and gives the recovery process a boundary worth defending.

This is the invariant: a run is either a candidate for restore or it is not. A scheduler success message is not evidence. A database dump that finished while the upload archive was still being assembled is not a backup.

Give every run a unique UTC identifier, and put that identifier in every key. For example:

The prefix is not a folder abstraction that makes consistency appear by magic. It is a naming contract. backups/production/20260811T020000Z/ should contain the database export, the receipt archive, and a manifest only after both payloads have been validated and stored. Keep the environment in the path so an operator cannot confuse staging evidence with production evidence during a stressful recovery.

The manifest should record the run ID, the exact object keys, byte counts, checksums produced by the backup worker, and the database export timestamp. It should also say which upload inventory the archive represents. That last field matters: a receipt row may exist in the database while its original object is absent, or the reverse may be true after a failed deletion workflow.

Short rule: no manifest, no restore candidate.

There is a consistency limit here. A nightly snapshot normally has a point-in-time boundary for the database, but user uploads arrive continuously. Decide what “complete” means before writing code: for example, include every receipt whose database record was committed before the export cutoff, and record any later objects for the next run. The exact policy depends on the application’s transaction model. I’m not sure a single archive can prove that relationship by itself; the manifest and an application-level inventory check are what make the claim testable.

The write path should have four states: planned, payloads stored, manifest committed, and verified. Only the third state is eligible for restore, and only the fourth should trigger retention cleanup. This gives operators a clear failure boundary when a worker is killed halfway through a large archive.

I would choose the third row for the game receipt workflow and keep the bucket private. The catch is that it is not suitable when the primary requirement is anonymous, permanent delivery of public media; a public distribution store or a separate delivery path is the better boundary there. Do not make the backup copy carry that convenience requirement.

Object storage also does not answer every durability question. The bucket may be durable while the design still has one failure domain, one credential, or one region. If the recovery objective includes a regional disaster, create and test a secondary-copy process. If the audit requirement includes immutability, select storage controls and permissions that prevent the backup identity from deleting its own evidence. The capability has to be verified against the actual policy, not inferred from the word “backup” in a product screen.

The storage client is deliberately abstract in this example. The application should bind put_bytes to the chosen object-storage SDK or HTTP implementation, while keeping the ordering and key contract unchanged. This is the part worth testing.

The manifest write is the publication step. A failed payload write must fail the job and leave no manifest; a failed manifest write must not be converted into a success by a scheduler wrapper. Retry policy belongs in the storage adapter, with bounded retries and logs that include the run ID but never receipt contents or credentials.

Before this function runs, the worker still needs a scheduler lock or queue policy so two nightly workers cannot claim the same run. Object keys are useful identifiers, but they are not a substitute for coordination. The job should also retain its local temporary files until the remote objects have been checked, then remove them according to the host’s disk policy.

A restore test should run against an isolated database and an isolated object-storage prefix. The sequence is intentionally boring:

The sixth check is where delivery simplicity gets challenged. A file that can be downloaded by a storage administrator is not necessarily accessible to the audit service, and a file that the audit service can read is not necessarily safe to expose to a game client. Test both authorization decisions. For browser delivery, use an application-controlled, time-limited access mechanism rather than turning the backup prefix into a public asset path.

The rejected design is a single latest/ prefix updated by independent database and upload jobs. It is valid for disposable exports where a new artifact replaces the old one and no relational reference must be reconstructed. It is not suitable for a full app restore: a timeout after the database upload can leave a fresh dump next to yesterday’s receipts, and a successful listing can still tell no one whether the pair is complete.

Lifecycle expiration can remove old run prefixes, but lifecycle configuration is retention automation, not a restore test. Keep a retention review that asks which manifests are complete, which copies are in the secondary location, and which restore drills still meet the recovery objective. Storage pricing also varies by storage class, request type, retrieval, and transfer; cost should be measured from the workload rather than used as the primary architectural argument.

If the access policy, inventory semantics, or disaster-recovery target cannot be stated in one page, the backup design is not finished. More automation will not repair an undefined restore boundary.
