#9748. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

#9745. Claude Fable 5.2 vs Opus 5.5: Is 2 the price worth it

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9. It's the new top of the Claude lineup, aimed at the hardest coding and reasoning work, and it costs twice as much per token as Claude Opus 5.5.

So the useful question isn't "is it better?" Anthropic's own numbers say it usually is. The question is when it's worth 2× the price, and what changes in your code if you switch.

This post covers what's new, the real price difference, the API details that will bite you on migration, and a simple way to decide. Everything here comes from Anthropic's announcement and docs unless it says otherwise.

Anthropic positions Fable 5.2 for "demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work". Compared with Fable 5.1, Anthropic says it:

There's also Claude Mythos 5.2, the same underlying model without the cybersecurity and biology safeguards. It's limited to organisations in Anthropic's verification programs, so for most developers, Fable 5.2 is the one you'll use.

These are from Anthropic's launch table, run at each model's highest effort with Fable's safeguards on. They're lab-reported, not independent, so treat them as a starting point for your own evals.

Two things stand out. The jump from Fable 5.1 is large on long agentic tasks. And Opus 5.5 still wins one row, AA-Briefcase Elo, so "newer and pricier" doesn't mean better at everything.

Fable 5.2 is cheaper than Fable 5.1 was ($10 / $50), but still exactly double Opus 5.5 per token. Batch requests are 50% off on both. Fable also has a fast mode at $16 / $80 that Anthropic says runs up to 2.5× faster.

Per token isn't the whole story, though. A stronger model can finish a task in fewer turns and with fewer retries, so it can cost less per task even at a higher per-token price. That's why the number to track is cost per successful task, not cost per token.

Both models have adaptive thinking always on, and you control how hard they think with the effort parameter. But their defaults are different: Fable 5.2 defaults to high, Opus 5.5 to medium.

So if you compare them with no settings, you're comparing Fable thinking harder against Opus thinking less. Some of the quality gap, and a lot of the cost gap, comes from that alone.

This type-checks against @anthropic-ai/sdk 1.8.0. Two notes on it:

Allowed effort values are low, medium, high, xhigh and max. Anthropic's advice for Fable 5.2: start at high, try xhigh for the hardest long-running work once you've measured a gain, and keep max for testing the ceiling.

If you're swapping the model ID in existing code, check these first. Each one is from the Fable 5.2 docs:

Anthropic's own model guide is refreshingly direct: start with Opus 5.5 for most workloads, and use Fable 5.2 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when Opus 5.5 at higher effort still falls short on your evals.

In practice, that gives you a simple test:

If Fable passes tasks Opus fails, or finishes in fewer turns, it can pay for itself. If both pass, Opus at half the price is the better default.

We gave both models the exact same prompt and recorded them side by side. [EDITOR: add the prompt, the effort setting used for each model, and 2–3 sentences on what you saw, then link the reel. Don't add numbers you didn't measure.]

One prompt isn't an eval, so treat it as a first impression, not a verdict.

New models will keep arriving every few months. The part that lasts is having your own evals and a workflow that doesn't depend on any single model. If you want to build that workflow properly, it's what our Agentic Engineering course is about.

Which model are you running as your default right now, and what would make you switch?

Sources: Anthropic: Claude Fable 5.2 · Claude docs: Models overview · Claude docs: Effort · Claude docs: Fable 5.2 overview · MacRumors: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.2

#9742. How to chase an unpaid invoice in Australia without losing the client (3 message templates)

Chasing an unpaid invoice feels awkward, especially when the client is someone you want to keep. The good news is that most late payments are not deliberate. Invoices get lost in an inbox, sent to the wrong person, or sit in an accounts queue. A short, polite, well-timed message fixes most of them.

This is the three-step approach I suggest for Australian sole traders and small businesses: a friendly nudge, a clear ask, then a firm but fair final reminder. Copy the templates, replace the [brackets], and send them by SMS or email.

A lot of delays come from the invoice, not the client. Before sending any reminder, check that:

Hi [Name], I think tax invoice [#] for $amount, due [date], may have slipped through. Could you check when it will be paid? Bank details are on the invoice. Thanks! [Your name]

Now you ask for a date, and you make it easy to say yes.

Subject: Invoice [#] - $[amount], now [x] days overdue

Hi [Name], I am following up on invoice [#] for $amount, now [x] days past our agreed [14]-day terms. I have attached it again in case the first one went to spam, and our ABN [ABN] is on it. Please pay by [date] or let me know what is holding it up. If something on the invoice is wrong, tell me and I will fix it today.

This one is direct but still professional. Do not threaten, and do not mention fees or formal steps unless they are in your signed terms.

Subject: Final reminder - invoice [#] for $[amount]

Hi [Name], I have not had a reply to my last two messages about invoice [#] for $amount. I would like to settle this without further steps, so please pay in full by [date] or call me on [phone] to agree a payment date. Until it is paid I will have to pause any new work. I would rather keep working together, so a quick reply is all I need.

I put together a free one-page version of these three messages, and a bigger Invoice Reminder Kit with more templates for before-the-due-date nudges, final notices, payment plans, disputes and a 30-day chase calendar. They are written in plain Australian English for tradies, cleaners, freelancers and other small operators. You can find the kits here: https://payhip.com/AussieSmallBizKits

If you use these templates and have a version that works better for you, I would like to hear it in the comments.

#9739. One Prompt, Every Log: Triage Production Issues Faster with MCP

Production issues aren't painful because fixing bugs is hard. They're painful because finding where the bug originated can take hours.

This is where MCP (Model Context Protocol) comes in. MCP is an open standard that allows AI assistants to connect with external tools and data sources, such as databases, monitoring platforms, application logs, and project management tools. It enables AI to interact with these systems and gather the context needed to investigate complex issues.

Hi I'm Shakti, a Software Engineer at a bug healthcare company. Recently I've been working closely with production issues and I've realized one thing time is everything when dealing with production incidents.

The real challenge isn't just fixing the bug. It's identifying where it originated, performing Root Cause Analysis (RCA), and reproducing the issue in lower environments.

All these steps can be extremely time-consuming.

Here are some practical tips on how you can use AI to triage production issues faster, identify root causes, and save valuable debugging time.

Start by identifying all the tools you manually use while triaging production issues.

Basically think about every tool you manually open when investigating a production issue and check whether an MCP is available for it.

Having an MCP integration doesn't automatically mean you have access to everything.

Check whether your account has the required permissions to access these tools, especially production databases, monitoring dashboards, application logs, and Jira projects.

Make sure you follow your organization's security and access policies. Prefer read-only access wherever possible.

Once you've identified the required MCP servers and verified your permissions, connect them to your primary AI harness or the AI assistant you use daily.

For example, this could be Claude, Cursor, or another AI environment that supports MCP integrations.

Now that you've connected all the tools, verify that your AI assistant can actually communicate with them.

Don't move forward until you've verified that the integrations are working as expected.

Create a separate project in your AI harness specifically for production issue triaging.

Give this project a detailed system prompt that defines the AI's role as an experienced Production Support Engineer who understands debugging, root cause analysis, log investigation, and issue reproduction.

Important: Instruct the AI not to assume a root cause without evidence. It should clearly distinguish confirmed findings from hypotheses.

Simply take the Jira ticket associated with the production issue and pass it to your dedicated AI project.

Your AI assistant can start investigating the issue using all the connected MCP tools, correlate information across different systems, and generate an investigation report.

Instead of manually switching between Jira, Grafana, databases, and log management platforms, you now have one place to coordinate the investigation.

The goal isn't to replace your debugging skills with AI. It's to eliminate repetitive investigation work so you can focus on understanding and resolving the actual problem.

AI won't magically fix every production issue, but with the right MCP integrations, context, and instructions, it can significantly reduce the time spent on investigation and debugging.

Stop spending hours collecting logs and switching between tools. Start using AI to connect the dots.

#9738. Solving the Erasure / Receipt Trilemma in AI Memory and RAG

Why delete_all(user_id=...) breaks GDPR compliance in practice — and how length-prefixed salted Merkle documents, two-tier AES-256-GCM crypto-shredding, and two-direction benchmarks close the gap.

Most vector stores (Qdrant, Chroma, Pinecone, pgvector) and agent memory layers (Mem0, Letta, LangMem) make storing facts and scoping simple queries by user_id straightforward. When a user invokes GDPR Article 17 ("Right to be Forgotten") or an enterprise client demands verifiable offboarding, three failure modes appear silently:

Failure 1: The Erasure / Receipt Trilemma

Imagine an onboarding call transcript or clinical intake note containing facts about two people:

"Priya Raman joined Acme in 2019 as a logistics analyst. Marcus Webb owns a bookshop in Leeds." Your RAG pipeline indexes that transcript and gives Marcus a cryptographic provenance receipt binding his fact to the document's flat SHA-256 hash and UTF-8 byte offsets.

Now Priya requests erasure. A flat document hash forces an impossible trilemma:

Redact or delete the transcript -> Priya's data is gone, but Marcus's SHA-256 receipt breaks forever because both the document digest and every byte offset shifted. Keep the transcript intact so Marcus's receipt verifies -> Priya's PII stays on disk permanently. Failure 2: Derived & Cross-Bucket Memory Leaks

Suppose an agent synthesizes a weekly summary:

"Riverside handoff: triage routing pairs with pharmacy inventory." Because summaries belong to "team_acme" rather than "priya", calling delete_all(user_id="priya") deletes Priya's raw memories — and leaves derived summaries, graph links, and append-only audit logs surfacing her context under a team namespace.

Failure 3: Zombie Re-Ingestion and Fake Compliance Metrics

Zombie syncs (webhook retries, backup imports, stale ETL jobs) re-ingest Priya minutes later under slightly different normalization ("Priya Raman" vs "priya"). Trivial 0-leak metrics: Any benchmark that only measures "leak rate" rewards wiping everything — destroying innocent bystanders' memories alongside the erased subject gives 0 leaks on paper while corrupting your store.

Ember (ember-custody) wraps an existing store (Mem0, LangChain/Chroma/Qdrant vector stores, or SQLite) without rewriting your retrieval model:

A. Salted Length-Prefixed RFC 6962 Merkle Documents (merkle.py)

Instead of hashing the whole document flatly, Ember splits a source into sentence/line/custom leaves, generates a fresh 128-bit random nonce per leaf, and hashes:

leaf_hash = SHA-256(0x00 || uint32_be(len(nonce)) || nonce || leaf_bytes) node_hash = SHA-256(0x01 || left_32 || right_32) Length-prefixing nonce prevents boundary ambiguity between (nonce, text) and ("", nonce + text). RFC 6962 0x00 vs 0x01 domain separation + strict positional proof-walk checks block second-preimage tree-geometry spoofing. On erasure: Ember strips Priya's leaf text and nonce, retaining only Priya's leaf_hash. The tree root stays identical, offline dictionary confirmation on common sentences fails (nonce is gone), and Marcus's receipt still verifies bit-for-bit against the redacted document using zero external dependencies (verify.py). B. Zero-Plaintext Append-Only Ledger + Two-Tier Crypto-Shredding (keystore.py, vault.py)

Append-only SQLiteLedger (WAL, synchronous=FULL) hashes an unbroken SHA-256 chain over encrypted subjects, text, quote, and caller metadata (AES-256-GCM bound via AAD to (tenant_id, item_id, field, key_ref)). Direct records encrypt under an opaque subject CEK (subject:subj_). Shared and derived_from records automatically compute the transitive ancestor set of all contributors and encrypt under a tracked per-record DEK (record:) indexed under every contributing subject. Erasing Priya redacts shared source leaves and destroys both Priya's CEK and every derived/shared DEK before calling external vendor delete() (so even a network timeout never leaves local decryption keys alive, and retries safely sweep pending IDs). From-zero ledger replay remains 100% tamper-evident while yielding [erased] and {} for all of Priya's items — leaving innocent bystanders decrypted and retrievable. C. Keyed Tombstones & Two-Direction Calibration (reducer.py, audit.py)

Vault-keyed HMAC-SHA256 tombstones block zombie re-ingestion with TombstonedSubjectError unless an explicit reconsent_id is recorded. erase() probes the raw backing store directly (adapter.search()) and refuses to issue an Ed25519 ErasureCertificate (ErasureIncomplete) if any residue still surfaces. The built-in adversarial suite tests 12 subjects × 7 attack categories (204 probes) while co-gating bystander retrieval survival and redacted Merkle receipt verification: Naive user_id-only baseline: 204/204 probes leak Ember wrapper: 0/204 probes leak, 100% bystander memories survive, 100% bystander receipts verify offline, 100% from-zero replays stay content-free.

Cryptography cannot erase data you already leaked out-of-band. Every certificate explicitly records trust boundaries (trust_boundary in ErasureCertificate):

Separate your keys from ledger backups: Crypto-shredding only protects pre-existing snapshots if key_dir (or your KMS/HSM KeyStore) was never backed up alongside ledger.db. External timestamp anchoring: Without configuring a TimestampAnchor (RFC 3161 TSA or public transparency log), a malicious root operator holding both ledger.db and ed25519.json can rewrite history coherently. Unanchored certificates explicitly declare externally_timestamped: false. Unlinked copy-paste residue: Structural lineage catches everything written via subjects and derived_from plus optional leaf_predicate sweeps; unlinked copies still trigger fail-closed rejection via probes.

#9736. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9734. How to Get Free Devnet SOL in 2026 (and Why solana airdrop Fails Now)

Posted on Nov 11 • Edited on Nov 11 • Originally published at solstack.xyz

Most Solana tutorials still start the same way: install the CLI, make a keypair, run solana airdrop 2. Run that against devnet today (CLI 4.2.2 here) and you get this:

The message blames a rate limit, so the natural move is to wait and try again later. For us it failed the same way a day later. We ran into this while funding test wallets for our own tools, and the cause turned out to be something waiting can't fix.

The CLI's airdrop command is a thin wrapper around one RPC method, requestAirdrop. Call that method yourself and the node gives a much clearer answer:

HTTP 410, Gone: the RPC faucet is closed on this cluster. Both api.devnet.solana.com and api.testnet.solana.com gave that answer on 11 November 2026. web3.js 1.99.0 hits the same wall, because connection.requestAirdrop() sends the same call:

So the airdrop built into the public RPC is switched off. A setup script or a test suite that asks the public endpoint for SOL stops at that line, and it will keep stopping there until the SOL comes from somewhere else.

Three ways to get test SOL still work. Which one fits depends on whether you're clicking through an app in a browser or running code.

A web faucet is a page that sends devnet SOL to an address out of a wallet somebody keeps funded. We run one, the Solstack Devnet Faucet, so people can try our tools on devnet before they spend real SOL.

The SOL shows up a few seconds later, with a Solscan link to the transfer. When we timed a request on 11 November it came back in 4.8 seconds. Each wallet address, and each IP, gets one request every 8 hours.

The whole request on video, in one minute:

The Solana Foundation runs a web faucet too, at the address the RPC error points to. Its page lists a maximum of 2 requests every 8 hours, and a higher limit if you sign in with GitHub.

If it's code that needs the SOL, and especially if that code runs in CI, skip devnet. The CLI ships with solana-test-validator, a single-node cluster on your own machine whose faucet has no rate limit:

That's the command that fails on devnet, and here it hands over 100 SOL in one go. requestAirdrop works from web3.js as well once the connection points at http://127.0.0.1:8899.

A local validator starts out empty, though. Your own program has to be deployed to it, and anything you rely on from devnet has to be copied in when it starts:

Tests that used to open with a devnet airdrop are better off here anyway. They stop depending on a faucet that somebody else can close.

Devnet SOL moves like any other SOL. If a teammate has some, or another wallet of yours does, one transfer covers it:

The last flag is needed because the CLI won't send to an address that holds no SOL unless you tell it to. This is how we fund the throwaway wallets in our own test runs: one funded wallet pays the rest.

A long way. Fees on devnet are the same as on mainnet: 5,000 lamports per signature, and a new token account takes a deposit of 1,488,440 lamports, about 0.0015 SOL. One SOL covers that deposit for roughly 670 token accounts.

For a sense of scale, on 10 November we ran our tools end to end on devnet. That run created a token, burned some of it, locked some, sent two multisends, opened two liquidity pools, added and removed liquidity, and launched a coin on a launchpad. All of it used about 0.55 SOL.

Devnet SOL has no value and can't be moved to mainnet, and the network can be reset, so there's little point in stockpiling it.

A faucet is a server that holds a funded keypair and signs a transfer when asked. The core of ours is a few lines in a Cloudflare Worker:

One bug from ours might save you some time. The first version waited for the transfer with connection.confirmTransaction(). That call listens on a WebSocket subscription, and inside a Worker the subscription never answered. The SOL landed in about a second. The request then sat there until the blockhash expired, roughly 38 seconds later, and reported "Send failed" for a transfer that had gone through.

The same request now answers in three to five seconds. On any serverless runtime, check that your confirmation step doesn't need a socket to stay open.

You'll also want a limit per address and per IP, or a single script will empty the wallet.

With SOL in the wallet, devnet is the place to rehearse anything you'd pay for on mainnet. Creating a token, sending an airdrop to a list and opening a liquidity pool all work there the way they do on mainnet.

Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

#9729. From Booking Requests to Confirmed Bookings: Designing Reliable Server-Side Events

A form submission is easy to track. A confirmed booking is harder.

In booking-based businesses, the customer may submit a request, reserve multiple seats, change plans, or cancel before attending. If all of those actions are counted as conversions, marketing reports can look successful while overstating actual business outcomes.

I worked on this problem in a booking attribution project where the goal was to connect campaign information, booking requests, CRM status changes, and analytics events.

This article describes the event-design decisions and testing approach. The code examples are simplified illustrations, not copies of production code.

The first challenge was semantic, not technical.

These stages are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A request tells us that someone expressed interest. A confirmation tells us that the business secured a booking. Attendance tells us something different again.

The tracking model must preserve those distinctions.

In our project, the primary marketing outcome was a confirmed booking, not simply a form submission.

Rather than sending an indistinguishable conversion every time something changes, define separate event types.

A useful event record might look like this:

This is an illustrative schema, not an actual customer record.

A confirmation should be generated from the actual booking state, not inferred from a thank-you page.

The implementation connects several parts of an existing booking system.

The website captures a request. The booking system remains responsible for booking status. The integration layer turns relevant state changes into analytics events.

This separation matters because marketing tools should not decide whether a customer has been confirmed. That decision belongs to the business system.

The server-side layer can then provide consistent delivery, validation, and retry handling.

Duplicate events are one of the easiest ways to corrupt conversion reporting.

Processing the same business event twice should not produce two business conversions.

For example, an idempotency key can combine the booking ID, transition type, and a transition version:

Conceptually, the server-side processing logic becomes:

The event record and its queue entry should be created reliably together. A retry should reuse the same event identity rather than create a new conversion.

It is also important to distinguish accepted by an API from visible in an analytics report. Those are separate verification steps.

One booking request can cover multiple people.

Suppose a customer requests three seats and the booking is confirmed.

If the dashboard reports three bookings instead of three seats, the result is misleading.

A correct report needs explicit metric definitions.

This is especially important for events, appointments, group activities, and other businesses where one customer action can represent several participants.

Campaign parameters are useful, but they should only be processed and forwarded to analytics platforms when the applicable consent requirements are satisfied.

In this implementation, consent is part of the tracking flow rather than an afterthought.

There is also a difference between knowing the campaign associated with a booking request and identifying the exact Instagram conversation that produced it.

Those are different levels of attribution.

The current system can preserve available campaign information and report booking statuses. It does not establish a verified one-to-one match between every individual Instagram Direct conversation and a specific booking.

Reporting should communicate that boundary instead of implying a level of certainty that the data cannot support.

A successful network request does not prove that the overall tracking implementation is correct.

Testing should cover the complete path from an initial booking request to the final business status.

Test records must also be distinguishable from real business results.

In the real project, some screenshots and counts come from integration tests. They demonstrate configured workflows, not proven increases in customers, sales, or revenue.

A useful conversion-tracking system is not simply one that sends more events.

It is one that answers precise questions:

When these questions are answered, analytics becomes much more useful for operational decisions.

I documented the real project, including implementation screenshots and its current limitations, in this booking attribution case study.

The broader principle applies beyond bookings: track confirmed business outcomes as distinct states, and test the entire data path before trusting a conversion report.

#9727. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9725. Fleet software for mixed robot dog, UGV and drone inspection teams

Posted on Nov 11 • Originally published at yuanzhirobot.com • Fully Autonomous

Short answer: there is rarely one off-the-shelf product that runs a Unitree or DEEP Robotics quadruped, a Clearpath or AgileX UGV and a DJI drone as one team. What works in practice is a thin common layer: an edge agent on each robot that translates its vendor SDK into a shared mission and telemetry format, one site map with a common coordinate frame, a server that assigns inspection points and stores results, and a single operator view. Most of the effort goes into map alignment, data formats and network behaviour, not into the dashboard.

Each platform family ships with a different control interface. Unitree quadrupeds such as the Go2 EDU and B2 are programmed through unitree_sdk2 over DDS. Clearpath UGVs (Husky, Jackal, Warthog) run ROS 2 natively. AgileX bases (Scout, Hunter, Bunker, Tracer) expose a CAN interface with ROS drivers on top. DJI enterprise drones are reached through the Payload SDK on the aircraft, the Mobile SDK on the controller or the Cloud API used by docks. Boston Dynamics Spot uses its own gRPC-based SDK. Vendor fleet tools usually manage only their own robots, so a site that mixes brands ends up with three apps, three maps and three report formats unless something sits above them.

Unitree Go2 EDU with a YUANZHI ROBOTICS sensor payload (3D render)

Four-wheel UGV payload design with a mast-mounted LiDAR and gimbal camera (3D render)

Keep ROS 2 and DDS traffic inside each robot. DDS discovery over 4G/5G or site Wi-Fi is fragile, so robots talk to the server through a small agent using MQTT or HTTPS for commands and telemetry and WebRTC or RTSP for video. The agent runs on the robot's payload computer; a Jetson Orin NX 16GB module (listed at 157 TOPS) leaves room for SLAM, detection and video encoding at the same time. Results are buffered locally and uploaded when the link returns, so a dead spot in a tunnel does not lose data. For remote sites a 5G module such as the Quectel RM520N-GL (3GPP Release 16) gives a usable uplink, but the mission must still finish safely if the link drops. Our 5G remote control guide covers that part in more detail.

If all robots come from one vendor, start with that vendor's tool. If the fleet is mixed, check whether a commercial fleet platform already has adapters for your exact models and SDK versions; adapters for quadrupeds are less common than for UGVs and drones. Building is justified when you have site-specific tasks (gauge reading on your panel types, gas alarm rules, integration with your maintenance system or SCADA) or when data must stay on-premises. A realistic build keeps the shared layer small and puts robot-specific logic in the agents, so adding a new platform means writing one adapter rather than touching the server.

DJI Matrice 350 RTK with a YUANZHI ROBOTICS sensor payload (3D render)

YUANZHI ROBOTICS builds payloads and software for quadrupeds, UGVs and drones, including edge agents, mapping and navigation, inspection-point logic and operator consoles. You can sketch the hardware for each robot in the payload configurator, review platform pages such as Unitree Go2 EDU, Clearpath Husky A200 and DJI Matrice 350 RTK, and read about our robot autonomy, inspection robot and drone payload services. For deciding which robot should handle which job, see UGV vs robot dog for inspection.

Written by the engineering team at YUANZHI ROBOTICS. Originally published at yuanzhirobot.com.

#9720. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9718. How I Learned to Share Ownership With My Product Manager

I’m an experienced product designer who loves science and the human side of technology ⭐️

I’m an experienced product designer who loves science and the human side of technology ⭐️

I’m an experienced product designer who loves science and the human side of technology ⭐️

Building a creative partnership takes more than putting two strong specialists on the same project.

You can be a brilliant designer, an experienced analyst, or a product manager who seems to have an answer for everything. Working with other people can amplify your expertise—or make it surprisingly difficult to put it to use.

I have spent seven years at Yandex, working alongside highly capable people. I have also watched misunderstandings between those people turn straightforward tasks into complicated negotiations.

Expertise does not automatically make collaboration easier. Sometimes, it gives each person more reasons to believe they are right.

I learned that lesson through a conflict I helped create.

While working at Yandex Market, I often took the lead in my partnership with a product manager. I answered product questions, defended our decisions, and proposed alternatives.

My partner seemed less experienced to me. He needed more time to gather his thoughts, while I was quick to jump into a discussion. So I decided, on behalf of both of us, that I would do the talking.

From my perspective, I was helping us move faster.

Eventually, we had a conflict. Through several conversations, I realized that taking over was making him less confident. He had fewer opportunities to explain his reasoning and demonstrate his expertise. I interpreted his hesitation as a reason to step in again.

We discussed what each of us needed. He wanted to present and defend the product rationale himself. I wanted design considerations to have a meaningful place in the decisions.

We changed how we approached product reviews, introduced regular one-on-ones, and became more attentive to each other’s needs within the project.

The problem had never been a shortage of ideas. I had assumed that my way of contributing worked for both of us.

That experience made me revisit my earlier work in advertising agencies, where projects often revolved around a creative pair. Two specialists brought different strengths and developed ideas together. When the partnership worked, they could produce strong work quickly.

I started applying that approach more deliberately to product management and design.

Of course, a PM and designer are part of a larger team. Engineers, analysts, researchers, and other colleagues shape the outcome. But this particular partnership influences many early decisions: which problem to solve, what to explore, and what to test.

I recognize three recurring patterns. These are working dynamics, not fixed personality types.

The PM defines the problem, chooses a solution, and sets the pace. The designer joins when something needs to be drawn.

Work moves forward, but the team uses only part of the designer’s expertise. Questions about usability and alternative approaches arrive too late to influence the direction.

A useful change is to involve design while the problem is still being framed. The designer also needs to bring questions and proposals into that conversation.

The designer takes over framing, strategy, discussions, and presentations. The PM becomes less visible, while the designer accumulates responsibility.

Important tasks can fall through the cracks: who is coordinating with stakeholders, checking business assumptions, or deciding the scope of a release?

Clear ownership helps, provided both people respect it. If your partner owns part of a discussion, leave them time to respond— even when you already have an answer.

Each person can lead, question assumptions, and make room for the other’s expertise.

The designer might help turn an abstract request into a concrete problem. The PM might bring evidence or constraints that change the design direction.

Both need to be willing to adjust. A partnership cannot depend on one person doing all the adapting.

Compromise is sometimes necessary. Deadlines and resources are real, and not every disagreement needs a new workshop.

But I try to avoid settling too quickly for a solution where each person gives something up just to end the argument.

Stephen Covey’s idea of synergy and the third alternative offers a useful way to think about this: different perspectives can help people develop a solution that improves on their original proposals.

Consider a hypothetical disagreement. A PM wants to launch a complex flow quickly. The designer believes the proposed shortcuts will make it confusing.

They could remove a few screens and ship something that satisfies neither concern particularly well.

Or they could examine what the deadline is meant to achieve. If the immediate goal is to test one assumption, a smaller, focused experiment might provide the evidence without requiring the full flow.

That possibility only emerges when both people explain what matters to them and are willing to reconsider their approach.

For me, this is the most valuable part of a creative partnership: discovering an option neither person brought into the room.

A few habits help turn that intention into everyday work.

Earlier in my career, I often entered discussions with an answer ready. Now, I try to establish a shared understanding first:

These questions help the PM clarify the request and help me focus my effort.

Agree on who gathers evidence, coordinates with stakeholders, presents each part of the proposal, and follows up on open questions.

For me, the difficult part was honoring those agreements when I felt tempted to step in.

A productive meeting can still leave two people with different plans. Keep a short record of what you decided, why, who owns the next step, and what remains unresolved. If you defer an improvement, record what would trigger revisiting it.

An art director once told me brainstorming was a waste of time. I have repeatedly found that an hour of focused discussion can accomplish more than a week of messages. Bring a specific question and options to compare. Leave with a decision or a next step.

“You push too hard” gives someone little guidance.

A more useful formulation identifies the behavior, its impact, and a request: “When you answer questions about my work before I can respond, I lose the opportunity to explain my reasoning. Can I lead that part next time?”

That is an illustrative example, but the principle is practical: describe something the other person can recognize and change.

Project meetings tend to fill up with project problems. Regular one-on-ones create space to discuss the working relationship itself.

What went well? What was frustrating? Where did either person need more support? What should we try differently?

Positive feedback matters here, too. Your partner should know which contributions helped. These conversations require participation from both people. One person cannot maintain a healthy partnership alone.

Over the couple of years since I started practicing this approach, I have changed how I work.

I used to spend much more energy defending my ideas and proving my independence. I took on responsibility and found it difficult to share.

Now, I pay closer attention to each person’s strengths. I explain what I can contribute and where I can help. We work out where to combine our efforts and where to trust each other to lead. Our ideas have become stronger, and I have maintained good relationships with my team through large, difficult projects.

I still disagree, ask questions, and stand up for what I believe matters. I am not trying to be the perfect or most agreeable colleague. I want the people around me to have room to do their best work—and to build something together that none of us could have created alone.

#9717. Cursor AI Modes Explained: Agent, Plan, Debug, Multitask & Ask - Which One Should You Use?

AI coding tools are changing how we build software. But using an AI coding assistant effectively is not just about choosing a powerful model or writing a good prompt. It is also about understanding how to delegate work, when to let AI make changes, when to investigate a problem, and when to simply ask questions.

One tool that has made this distinction interesting is Cursor.

If you have been using Cursor, you have probably come across different modes: Agent, Plan, Debug, Multitask, and Ask.

They may look like different ways of interacting with the same AI assistant, but they serve different purposes.

Understanding these modes can significantly improve your development workflow, reduce unnecessary AI usage, and, more importantly, help you maintain control over the code being generated.

Agent mode is where most of the actual development happens.

Think of it as giving an AI developer a task and allowing it to investigate your codebase, determine which files need changes, implement the solution, run commands, and test whether the implementation works.

Unlike basic code completion, Agent can work across multiple files and handle tasks that require several steps.

For example, imagine you want to add an authentication system to an existing application.

Implement JWT authentication in the existing application. Include user registration, login, token validation middleware, password hashing, and appropriate API tests. Follow the existing project architecture and coding conventions.

However, there is something important to remember.

Agent mode does not mean you should surrender engineering judgment. Review the changes, understand the decisions, inspect the diffs, and verify the implementation.

AI can write code, but you remain responsible for the software you ship.

This is one of the most useful modes, especially when working on complex projects.

How many times have you asked an AI agent to implement something, only to realize halfway through that it misunderstood the architecture or requirements?

Instead of immediately writing code, Cursor first investigates the codebase, asks clarifying questions where necessary, and develops an implementation plan.

You get an opportunity to review the proposed approach before allowing the agent to build anything.

Imagine you are developing an invoice processing system that uses AI to extract information from uploaded documents.

I want to implement an AI-powered invoice extraction workflow. Before writing any code, investigate the existing architecture and create a detailed implementation plan covering document uploads, extraction, validation, database storage, error handling, and testing. Identify the files that will need modification and any architectural decisions we need to make.

Once satisfied, you can approve the plan and proceed with implementation.

My recommendation: For anything that touches several parts of your application, start with Plan mode.

It is much cheaper to correct a misunderstanding in a plan than to undo hundreds of lines of incorrectly implemented code.

Most AI coding assistants can read an error message, search the codebase, and suggest a fix.

But what happens when the problem is not obvious?

Consider an application where a payment occasionally fails. Sometimes the transaction succeeds, sometimes it times out, and sometimes the customer gets charged without receiving a confirmation.

Reading the code might not immediately reveal the problem.

Debug mode takes a more evidence-driven approach.

Rather than immediately changing code, Cursor investigates possible causes, develops hypotheses, and adds instrumentation to collect runtime information.

The biggest advantage is that you are not simply asking AI to guess what is wrong.

You are giving it an opportunity to investigate actual application behaviour.

That is a much better engineering approach.

This is one of the most interesting developments in Cursor.

Traditionally, you would give an agent a task, wait for it to finish, and then give it another task.

Cursor can use asynchronous subagents to divide work into independent tasks and execute them in parallel.

Instead of waiting for one agent to complete everything sequentially, you can delegate different parts of the work to multiple agents.

Imagine you are developing a SaaS application with three independent areas of work:

These tasks can potentially be handled concurrently, provided their dependencies and shared-file changes are managed appropriately.

Cursor's /multitask workflow allows you to parallelize requests instead of simply adding them to the queue.

You can also use the Build in Parallel option when working from an implementation plan. Cursor identifies independent tasks and executes them using asynchronous agents while respecting dependencies where necessary.

However, multitasking is not always the answer.

If three agents need to modify the same authentication service, database schema, or shared business logic, parallel execution can introduce conflicts and integration problems.

The key is identifying tasks that can genuinely run independently.

More agents do not automatically mean better engineering.

This is probably one of the most underrated modes, especially for developers who are learning a new codebase.

Ask mode is designed for exploration and understanding.

It allows you to ask questions about your project without having the AI automatically modify your files.

Think about joining an existing project with thousands of lines of code.

Before changing anything, you need to understand:

Instead of immediately asking Agent to modify the project, you can start with Ask mode.

Explain how the payment processing workflow works in this application. Trace the process from the API request to the database transaction and identify the services, controllers, and external integrations involved. Do not modify any files.

If you are learning software engineering while using AI coding tools, this mode is particularly valuable.

You should not just be interested in what AI has implemented. You should understand how and why it implemented it.

Rather than treating these modes as isolated features, I would combine them into a development workflow.

Suppose you are building a payment integration for a business application.

Start by understanding the existing payment architecture.

Ask Cursor to explain how payments currently work, where transactions are stored, and how external payment providers are integrated.

Ask Cursor to develop an implementation plan for the new payment provider integration.

Review the architecture, API endpoints, database changes, security considerations, and testing requirements.

Once the plan is approved, allow Agent to implement the integration.

Review the changes and ensure that the implementation follows the agreed architecture.

If the remaining work can be separated, delegate independent tasks such as documentation, test coverage, and separate frontend components to parallel agents.

If something fails unexpectedly, switch to Debug mode and investigate the actual runtime behaviour instead of repeatedly asking Agent to try another fix.

This approach introduces something important: structure.

You are not simply prompting an AI to write code. You are directing a software development process.

One mistake developers make when adopting AI coding tools is focusing too much on how much code the AI can generate.

But code generation is only one part of software engineering.

Cursor makes it easier to delegate implementation, investigate problems, and explore unfamiliar systems.

But the quality of the final product still depends on the decisions made throughout the development process.

I particularly like the distinction between Ask, Plan, Agent, and Debug because it encourages developers to think before making changes, understand before implementing, and investigate before fixing.

And with Multitask, we are moving towards a development workflow where engineers increasingly coordinate multiple AI agents rather than simply interact with one assistant.

The future of software engineering is not just about writing code faster. It is about becoming better at directing, reviewing, and validating the work being done by AI systems.

Learn the tools, understand the fundamentals, and never outsource your engineering judgment.

What is your most-used Cursor mode? Are you an Agent-first developer, or do you prefer planning and understanding the codebase before allowing AI to make changes?

I'd be interested to hear how other developers are incorporating these modes into their daily workflows.

#9715. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.
